Squatters versus adverse possession

Alabama treats these as two different things. Adverse possession is a slow claim to ownership under a statute in Title 6 of the Code of Alabama. Squatting, in the sense lawmakers meant in 2024, is a quick removal procedure for people who move into a dwelling with no right to be there. It lives in Chapter 9B of Title 35.

In real life they seldom overlap. Someone who broke into a vacant house last month has no realistic claim to title, yet you still need a lawful way to get them out. Someone who has used a lot for decades and paid tax on it may hold a real claim, and removal paperwork won't erase it.

If a stranger is living in your Alabama house, sort out which situation you're in before anything else. That decides whether you file a sworn affidavit with law enforcement, start a court case, or sit down with a title attorney before signing a sale contract.

What a claimant must prove for adverse possession

Under Alabama Code section 6-5-200, living on land isn't enough by itself. The claimant has to prove one of three things before adverse possession can create or defeat title.

  • A deed or other color of title was recorded with the county probate judge for 10 years before the lawsuit started.
  • The claimant, and anyone the claimant takes through, listed the land for taxes in the proper county every year for 10 years before the action, if the land is taxable.
  • The claimant got title by descent or devise from a predecessor who was in possession.

Time can be added together. If the claimant's recorded paper and that of the people he claims through total 10 years, he can rely on the combined period. An honest failure to list the land for tax, a slip in the description on the assessment, or an accidental omission of part of the parcel doesn't automatically sink the claim.

The section also protects older rights. It leaves alone a title that was already perfect by adverse possession before the Code was adopted, it preserves rights under sections 6-6-286 through 6-6-289, and it doesn't change how boundary disputes between neighbors are handled.

Removing a squatter from a dwelling

An owner or the owner's agent can ask law enforcement in the county where the dwelling sits to remove an unauthorized person. The request is a sworn affidavit under section 35-9B-2. Act 2024-237 added the chapter, and it borrows the criminal code's definition of a dwelling.

You sign the affidavit under penalty of perjury, so every statement must be true for your situation:

  • You own the dwelling or act as the owner's agent.
  • Someone entered and remains unlawfully and was never authorized to be there.
  • The person isn't a tenant or a holdover tenant.
  • You asked the person to leave, and they haven't.
  • The person isn't an immediate family member of the owner.
  • No litigation about the dwelling is pending between you and that person.

The statutory form goes further. It states that any lease the person shows is fraudulent, that the person isn't on title unless title fraud occurred, and that notice was hand delivered or posted on the front door with proof of the date and time attached. You also attach a copy of your government-issued ID, or papers showing your authority if you're an agent.

Before filing, post or hand deliver a notice at the dwelling telling the person to leave immediately. It must give the street address of the law enforcement agency that will receive the affidavit, and a copy goes in with the affidavit.

What law enforcement does next

The agency starts by confirming you're the record owner or an authorized agent and that you appear entitled to relief. After at least 24 hours from receiving the affidavit, it serves a notice to vacate immediately. Service can be by hand to anyone in the home or by posting on the front door, per section 35-9B-3.

Officers also try to identify everyone inside and record the names on the return of service. Where it fits, an officer can arrest someone found in the dwelling for trespass, burglary, theft, another crime, or an outstanding warrant. The agency may charge no more than $50 to process the affidavit.

StageWho acts
Post or hand deliver notice at the dwellingOwner or agent
Submit sworn affidavit with ID and proof of noticeOwner or agent
Verify record owner, wait at least 24 hours, serve notice to vacateLaw enforcement
Identify occupants, arrest if warrantedLaw enforcement
Charge a processing fee of $50 or lessLaw enforcement agency

What happens if the affidavit is wrong?

The person who signs carries the risk. Section 35-9B-6 lets a wrongfully removed person sue the affiant. Remedies include getting possession back, actual costs and damages, punitive damages of triple the fair market rent of the dwelling, court costs and reasonable attorney fees.

The affidavit form says as much. By signing, you acknowledge that a removed person may sue over false statements or misuse of the procedure, with liability for actual damages, penalties, costs and attorney fees. If you can't tell whether the occupant is a tenant, a guest or a relative, talk to a lawyer before you sign.

Chapter 9B also shields utilities that follow the usual court route. Under section 35-9B-7, a utility may rely on or require a writ of possession from the landlord tenant or ejectment chapters when it decides whether to cut service at a dwelling, and it isn't liable for acting on that writ. Shutting off power yourself to push someone out is a bad shortcut.

When the occupant is a tenant or holdover

The squatting affidavit excludes tenants and holdover tenants by its own terms. If the person ever had a lease, paid rent, or stayed past the end of a term, you must use the landlord tenant process in Chapter 9A and file for possession in court.

Under the Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act, a landlord can sue for possession against a tenant who stays without consent after the term expires or the lease ends. A willful holdover can lead to recovery of up to three months of periodic rent or actual damages, whichever is greater, plus reasonable attorney fees.

The line between the two routes also affects a sale. Buyers and lenders want to know about any recorded claim, lease or pending case, and the squatting affidavit is off the table once litigation over the dwelling is already pending between you and the occupant.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy Alabama houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

Selling a house with an occupant or a title question

You can still sell an occupied house, but the route depends on who's inside, and the occupant question affects who can buy and how quickly. Before you list or accept a cash offer, do three things:

  1. Pull the recorded documents at the county probate office. Adverse possession runs through recorded deeds and tax listing, so an odd recorded paper or tax history on your parcel is worth knowing about.
  2. Write down how the occupant got in and when. The affidavit and any court filing both depend on a clear timeline.
  3. Put the notice, proof of delivery and any police paperwork in one folder.

When the person has no claim, Chapter 9B offers a path. When they hold a lease, a family tie, or a pending case, the path runs through court. In either case you can ask Cash Home Buyers CA for an offer on the house as it stands, and we'll tell you plainly how an occupant changes timing.

Title companies tend to ask for the same paperwork you'd gather anyway, so keeping that folder current saves days later. A buyer paying cash can often set a closing date around a court schedule.

Frequently asked questions

Can a squatter take ownership of my Alabama house?

Only by meeting section 6-5-200: recorded color of title for 10 years, annual tax listing for 10 years, or title by descent or devise from a predecessor in possession. Living in a house for a while doesn't transfer ownership.

Is there a faster way to remove a squatter than a full eviction?

Yes, for people who aren't tenants. Chapter 9B lets an owner or agent file a sworn affidavit with local law enforcement, which verifies ownership, waits at least 24 hours and serves a notice to vacate. Tenants, holdover tenants and immediate family are excluded.

How much can law enforcement charge to process the affidavit?

No more than $50 under section 35-9B-3(b).

What happens if I file against someone who is really a tenant?

You can be sued. A wrongfully removed person may recover possession, actual damages, triple the fair market rent as punitive damages, court costs and attorney fees under section 35-9B-6.

Can I sell my Alabama house while someone occupies it without permission?

If you hold title you can contract to sell, but an unresolved occupant affects terms and timing. Ask an Alabama attorney which removal route fits your facts before you sign a contract.

Alabama Landlord Tenant Law and Tenant Rights: Rules for Selling a Rental

Selling a Alabama House? Get a Cash Offer

We buy as-is.

Call or Text  (424) 435-2326


Last updated November 14, 2026.

Selling in Alabama?

The law that governs Alabama rentals

A single statute, the Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act, covers home rentals across the state. You will find it at Title 35, Chapter 9A, and it was enacted as Act 2006-316. Six articles organize it: general provisions, landlord obligations, tenant obligations, remedies, retaliatory conduct, and the effective date and savings provisions.

Squatting sits in a different chapter, 9B. When someone is living in a property without a lease or permission, begin with that chapter and not the rental rules.

Disclosure duty and who inherits it

Under Section 35-9A-202, the landlord, or whoever is authorized to sign leases for the landlord, must put in writing for the tenant, by the time the tenancy starts, the name of the property manager and of the owner or owner's agent who accepts legal papers and notices.

If you plan to sell, two points matter. The details must be kept up to date, and the section binds any later landlord, owner or manager. A rental buyer therefore inherits the duty, and an outgoing seller should pass on a clean record of what the tenant was told. Keep a dated copy of the written disclosure in your sale file.

Staying silent has a price. Whoever skips the disclosure becomes each landlord's agent for receiving notices and demands and for carrying out the landlord's duties under the chapter and the lease. That can pull a former or faraway owner into disputes they thought were behind them.

Repairs the landlord must make

Section 35-9A-204 is the source of the landlord's upkeep duties. Obey the building and housing codes that materially affect health and safety, fix what keeps the unit livable, and keep shared areas clean and safe.

  • Electrical, plumbing, sanitary, heating, ventilating and cooling systems, plus any appliances the landlord supplies, must work well and safely.
  • Garbage containers and removal are the landlord's job.
  • Running water, a reasonable supply of hot water and reasonable heat are owed, except where the building needs no heat or the tenant runs the system through a direct utility hookup.

Where a code duty is stricter than anything on the list, the code controls. Tenants lose these rights if they, a family member or a guest created the condition through a willful or negligent act.

Free, no-obligation offerTell us about your Alabama house and get a written cash offer within 24 hours.Get My Cash Offer →

Can a tenant agree to do repairs?

Sometimes. With a one-family house, the two sides can put in writing that the tenant handles garbage and water and named repairs, maintenance, alterations and remodeling.

Every other kind of dwelling faces tighter terms. A separate signed writing with adequate consideration is required, the work may not be what is needed to fix a code violation, and it may not shrink what the landlord owes other tenants. Tying the side deal to the lease itself is also off limits.

When the tenant of the house you are selling handles upkeep, a buyer will want that writing, because the statute requires it.

Terminating for unpaid rent or a violation

Section 35-9A-421 starts with a written notice from the landlord. It names a termination date seven or more business days after the tenant gets it, and the tenant can use that time to fix the problem.

Ground for ending the leaseWhat the statute requires
Material noncompliance with the leaseWritten notice naming the acts or omissions, ending the lease seven or more business days after receipt unless the tenant remedies the breach first
Unpaid rentWritten notice listing rent and late fees due; the lease ends seven or more business days after receipt if the money stays unpaid
Intentional misrepresentation of a material fact in the lease or applicationCannot be remedied or cured
Both grounds at onceThe unpaid rent period governs

The landlord can in addition pursue actual damages, attorney fees and an injunction.

Breaches a tenant cannot cure

The section also restricts cures: no more than two per 12-month stretch for any lease term, unless the landlord agrees in writing.

Certain acts are noncurable defaults, letting the landlord end the lease on seven days' notice with no right to remedy unless the landlord agrees:

  • Drug activity of any sort inside the unit or the shared areas.
  • Unlawful use or discharge of a gun or ammunition on the premises, other than self-defense and cases the statute lists.
  • A criminal assault on a tenant or a guest at the property, with the same self-defense and listed exceptions.
  • Repeating, within six months, substantially the same conduct that was already noticed and cured.
Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy Alabama houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

Selling a rental house with a tenant

Selling with a tenant in the house adds paperwork, and the statutes above set the baseline. Before closing, the buyer's attorney or title company typically reviews the lease, disclosure details, repair history and pending notices.

Collect these first:

  • The signed lease and any written maintenance deal with the tenant.
  • The disclosure naming the manager and owner or agent that your tenant was given.
  • Any termination notice and the day the tenant received it, because the seven business day count starts then.
  • Records of repairs you made as landlord and any code notices.

A sitting tenant does not always get in the way. Certain buyers want occupied rentals, while some owners prefer to sell vacant. Either way, the buyer's lender or attorney may ask how long the lease runs and whether the rent is current. A month-to-month lease or a tenant who has stopped paying changes how and when the tenancy can end, and that sets your timeline. An Alabama attorney can say which notice suits your facts.

Questions to settle before you sell

Rental sales go smoother when a few questions are answered early. Is the tenant current on rent, and is a notice out? Does the lease end soon, or will it run past the closing date? Were repairs made when the tenant asked, and is there a record? Is there a written maintenance agreement that a buyer would inherit?

Answers to these tell a buyer how much risk comes with the house. They also tell you whether to end the tenancy first, sell with the tenant in place, or choose a buyer who will take the house as it stands.

Cash sale of an occupied house

It can be done. Cash buyers skip mortgage underwriting and appraisals, and an investor who buys rentals can take on a house in whatever shape it is in.

That includes houses with repairs the landlord put off, tenants who pay late and untidy paperwork. Be honest about the lease, the tenant's status and any notice already served. To close and move on, request an offer on the house as is and decide later. Declining costs nothing.

You pick the closing dateClose in as little as 7 days or on the date that works for you, with no fees or commissions.Get My Cash Offer →

Frequently asked questions

How much notice does an Alabama landlord give for unpaid rent?

The landlord serves a written notice listing rent and late fees, and the lease can end seven business days after the tenant gets it. Pay in that window and the lease survives.

Can a tenant fix a lease violation after getting a notice?

Generally, before the notice period runs out. Two cures per 12 months is the cap without the landlord's written consent, and drug use, certain firearm violations and criminal assault cannot be cured at all.

What repairs must an Alabama landlord make?

Comply with health and safety codes, keep the unit livable, maintain electrical, plumbing, heating and cooling and any appliances provided, arrange garbage removal, and supply water, hot water and heat at reasonable levels, with a few exceptions.

Does a buyer of a rental take over the landlord's disclosure duty?

Yes. A successor landlord, owner or manager takes on that duty and can be held to it, and the details must be kept current.

Can a tenant agree to maintain the house?

In a one-family house, yes, by a written agreement on garbage, water and named repairs. Other dwellings need a separate signed writing, and the work cannot be what cures a code violation.

title: Alabama Eviction Notice Rules: Notice Types, Days and Selling the House
content:
Alabama Eviction Notice Rules: Notice Types, Days and Selling the House

Cash Home Buyers in Alabama
Cash Offer in 24 Hours
  • Alabama Eviction Notice Rules: inherited, behind on payments, tenants or repairs, we buy the house as-is
  • No fees, commissions or closing costs on a Alabama Eviction Notice Rules sale
  • Turn the Alabama Eviction Notice Rules offer down and you owe us nothing

Selling a Alabama House? Get a Cash Offer

We buy as-is.

Call or Text  (424) 435-2326


Last updated November 14, 2026.

Selling in Alabama?
We buy Alabama houses as-is, with no commission, no repairs and no closing costs to you.
Get My Cash Offer →

Notice periods by situation

How much warning a tenant gets turns on the landlord's reason. The act sets seven days as the floor, and the usual ceiling is 30 days, which applies when a landlord simply wants a month-to-month tenant out with no cause given. A written notice precedes any court filing, every time.

SituationNotice required
Unpaid rentWritten demand listing rent and late fees; the lease ends if they stay unpaid seven business days after receipt
Material lease breach or health and safety violationWritten notice describing the acts, with a termination date at least seven business days out
Noncurable default (listed acts)Seven days, and no right to cure unless the landlord agrees
Week-to-week tenancyWritten notice seven or more days ahead of the end date
Month-to-month tenancyWritten notice 30 or more days ahead of the periodic rental date

The first three rows come from Section 35-9A-421, subsections (b), (a) and (d). The last two come from Section 35-9A-441, subsections (a) and (b).

What a nonpayment notice must say

Put it on paper, hand it to the tenant, and list the rent and late fees owed. Section 35-9A-421(b) also requires a statement that the rental agreement will end seven or more business days after the tenant gets the notice.

If the tenant pays the whole demand in time, the problem is cured and the lease continues. If not, the agreement ends by operation of the statute, and the landlord may ask a court for possession.

A tenant can break the lease two ways at once, such as missing rent and committing a material breach. In that case the seven day nonpayment period controls, which spares the landlord from tracking two deadlines.

Notice for a material lease violation

Here the landlord writes down what the tenant did or failed to do and picks a termination date at least seven business days after the notice is received. Section 35-9A-421(a) reaches serious violations of the lease, lying on purpose about a material fact in the lease or application, and neglect of the tenant's health and safety duties under Section 35-9A-301.

A tenant who repairs the problem adequately before the end date keeps the lease. The one violation that can never be repaired is a deliberate lie about a material fact in the rental agreement or application.

Section 35-9A-421(c) lets the landlord also pursue actual damages, reasonable attorney fees and an injunction.

Free, no-obligation offerTell us about your Alabama house and get a written cash offer within 24 hours.Get My Cash Offer →

Violations with no chance to cure

Four kinds of conduct in Section 35-9A-421(d) are treated as defaults that cannot be cured, so a seven-day notice can end the tenancy. The statute says the list includes, but is not limited to:

  • Illegal drug activity of any kind in the unit or common areas, from growing and importing to supplying and using.
  • Unlawful handling or firing of a gun or ammunition on the property, other than in self-defense, defense of another or as Section 13A-3-23 allows.
  • A criminal assault on a tenant or guest there, with the same self-defense exceptions.
  • Repeating, within six months, much the same conduct the tenant already cured once.

The subsection also limits cures overall: no tenant may cure a breach of any lease term more than two times in 12 months without the landlord's written consent, whatever Section 35-9A-141 says.

Ending a month-to-month or week-to-week tenancy

Give written notice, with 30 days for a month-to-month arrangement and seven for a week-to-week one. Section 35-9A-441 lets landlord and tenant alike use it, so a tenant leaving follows the same periods.

The 30 days run back from the rental date named in the notice. To have a tenant out by the first of a month, deliver the notice no later than 30 days before it.

Nothing here accuses the tenant of anything. It works for an owner who is selling and just needs vacant possession, and the dates can be matched to a buyer's closing.

If the tenant stays after the notice ends

The landlord can sue for possession. If the tenant's stay is willful and in bad faith, Section 35-9A-441(c) opens the door to more: up to three months' periodic rent, or actual damages when those run higher, along with reasonable attorney fees.

One counterweight applies. If the landlord consents to the tenant's continued occupancy, Section 35-9A-161(d) governs instead.

Court steps beyond that point, including service, the seven day appeal window and the writ, belong to the eviction lawsuit itself.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy Alabama houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

Retaliation and notices

A notice may not be revenge. Section 35-9A-501 forbids discriminatory rent increases, service cuts, and suing or threatening to sue for possession when the reason is that the tenant did one of three protected things:

  • Reporting a health and safety violation to the agency that enforces the building or housing code.
  • Telling the landlord about a breach of the duty to maintain the premises under Section 35-9A-204.
  • Organizing or joining a tenants' union or similar group.

Proof of retaliation gives the tenant the remedies in Section 35-9A-407 and a defense in the possession case. Even so, a landlord may sue over unpaid rent, a code violation the tenant or a guest caused by carelessness, repairs that would in effect take the home from the tenant, or other material lease violations.

Returning the security deposit

Any unused deposit goes back to the tenant, together with a list of each deduction, within 60 days. Section 35-9A-201 permits the landlord to use the deposit for unpaid rent and for damage that comes from the tenant's failure to meet Section 35-9A-301. The written breakdown and the balance are due 60 days after the tenancy ends and possession is handed over.

Security of more than one month's periodic rent cannot be demanded, apart from pets, alterations or added liability risk. If a sale is in the works, mark that 60 day deadline on your calendar.

Does a notice help you sell the house?

A notice served correctly hands you a date to plan around, and some buyers will wait for it. Others hold off until the tenant has moved out.

Rentals with a notice out or a case pending are houses we look at too. Tell us the address and how far along things are, and we can discuss a closing date that works.

Before you call, gather the lease, a copy of any notice you served, the date the tenant received it, and a record of what rent is owed. Those four items show a buyer how much time and risk remain on the house.

You pick the closing dateClose in as little as 7 days or on the date that works for you, with no fees or commissions.Get My Cash Offer →

Frequently asked questions

How long is an Alabama eviction notice for unpaid rent?

The landlord must give a written notice listing rent and late fees, and the lease can end seven business days after the tenant receives it (Section 35-9A-421(b)).

How much notice ends a month-to-month tenancy in Alabama?

Thirty days in writing, counted back from the rental date in the notice (Section 35-9A-441(b)). Either side may give it.

Can an Alabama landlord skip the cure period?

For some conduct, yes. Drug activity, illegal gun use, criminal assault and a repeat of a cured breach inside six months are noncurable under Section 35-9A-421(d), which allows seven-day termination.

What can a landlord recover from a tenant who stays after the notice?

When the stay is willful and in bad faith, up to three months' rent or actual damages if higher, plus reasonable attorney fees (Section 35-9A-441(c)).

When does a landlord have to return the deposit in Alabama?

Within 60 days of the end of the tenancy and the handover of possession, along with an itemized list of deductions (Section 35-9A-201).
